turns: We want to run a two-week pilot in Harbour Hall library before the end of term.
Two weeks is enough if you decide now what would count as success. Pick one number, like the share of students who check the map before walking over. What number would make you call the pilot a win?
maybe 30% of students in the building using it at least once
30% is a fine bar for a first pilot. You'll need a rough count of who is in the building, so ask the library for their gate counts. Does Harbour Hall share its door-counter data?
they do, weekly
Then you can compare weekly gate counts with weekly map opens. Ask for the last four weeks too, so you have a baseline before the pilot starts. When does the pilot start?
the 12th, right before finals
Finals week will inflate usage, so treat that week as a stress test, not the baseline. Plan one week before finals and one during, and compare them.
We've been interviewing commuter students about where they study between lectures.
Commuters are a sharp segment because their time between lectures is fixed. What did the last three tell you about how they pick a study spot?
mostly they go wherever their friends are, or the café if the library's full
So the real competitor is the café, not another app. That matters for pricing: they already pay for a coffee to sit somewhere. How much do they spend at the café in a typical week?
one said like £15 a week lol
£15 a week is a strong anchor for the value of a seat. Ask the next five the same question, word for word, so the numbers are comparable. Who is next on your interview list?
two people from the engineering society on thursday
Good. Bring the £15 question, and one about what happens when the café is full too. Write down their exact words, not your summary.

conversations.opener: Hi Maya, good to see you. How did the library staff interviews go?
turns: Hi, it's Maya. I have a few minutes before my next class, so let's be quick.
Let's make it count, then. What's the one thing you want to leave this call with?
We're trying to decide between charging each library branch separately or one flat fee for the whole campus.
Per branch is easier to start, because each branch can say yes on its own. Who signs the cheque for each library branch, and who can block it?
Sorry to cut in, what would you charge for a short pilot instead?
For a short pilot, charge something small but real, like two hundred pounds for the term. A token price tells you whether they will pay at all.
How should we price per library? We have two libraries interested in the quiet-seat app.
Start from what each library already spends to keep study space open late. That budget is your anchor, not what students would pay. Who signs off on that budget at each branch?
Facilities holds it I think. The east library manager said £900 a term sounds fair.
£900 a term from one manager is a signal, not a price yet. Ask her to confirm it in an email with the term dates, so you have it in writing. What would make her say no?
probably if students complain about being tracked
Then privacy is the first objection to handle, before price. Write one short paragraph on what the sensors count and what they never store. Can you get that to her before Friday?
yeah tonight
Good. Keep it under 150 words and lead with the fact that you never store names. Once she replies, you'll know whether £900 holds.
the pitch is three minutes and I have fourteen slides
Fourteen slides in three minutes is a slide every thirteen seconds. Cut to five: problem, who has it, what you built, proof, ask. Which slide would you fight hardest to keep?
the traction one, 61 of 90 students said they'd use it
Keep it, but say it as a story: 61 of 90 students check a group chat to find a seat, and the map replaces that. What's your ask at the end of the pitch?
£5k from the innovation fund
Tie the £5k to the pilot: sensors for two libraries for one term. Judges fund a plan, not a wish. Can you say what the £5k buys in one sentence?
lab managers like $40 because it's under their card limit and skips procurement
Staying under the card limit is a real advantage, because procurement reviews take about six weeks. Who besides the lab manager has to approve a new tool?
the chemistry chair sometimes
Then the chair is the hidden veto. A one-page note on safety and expiry tracking would help her say yes. When could you get ten minutes with her?
she has office hours on wednesday
Use them. Bring one story of a reagent that expired unnoticed and what it cost. Keep the ask small: a one-month trial in one lab.
honestly I'm exhausted, my cofounder hasn't done anything this week and the demo is Monday
That's a lot to carry alone right before a demo. Let's make Monday smaller: what's the one thing the demo has to show?
that the map updates live
Then cut everything else from the demo script. A live map on one floor is enough. Who could sit in the library on Monday so the map changes while you present?
my flatmate maybe
Ask her today, so it's settled. And when the demo is done, it's worth a straight conversation with your cofounder about this week. How do you want to start that conversation with him?
the grant form has a 500 word limit for the impact section and I have two thousand words
Cut it to one claim and one number. The impact section needs who benefits and how you'll know. What's the single number you would measure?
hours saved finding a seat
Hours saved works if you can measure it in the pilot. Estimate it from the gate counts and survey ten students. Do you have a baseline for hours saved yet?
not really
Then run a quick baseline this week: ask ten students how long they spent looking for a seat yesterday. That's enough for the form.
We're thinking about selling Fit4Life to small gyms instead of to members directly.
Selling to gyms changes who you need to convince. A gym owner cares about retention, not workouts. How many gym owners have you actually spoken to?
three. two liked it, one said they already use mindbody
Mindbody is the incumbent you'll meet everywhere, so find out what the third owner would miss if he switched. What did the two who liked it say they'd pay?
one said maybe $49 a month
$49 a month from one owner is a starting point. Offer a 30-day trial at $49 and see whether she puts in a card. Which gym would you ask first?
